qs.q: A 50-year-old man with chronic hyperuricemia experiences a sudden, exquisitely painful attack of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. What is the initial molecular event following MSU crystal phagocytosis by synovial macrophages?
qs.e: When MSU crystals are phagocytosed by macrophages, they activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to the release of IL-1β and subsequent intense neutrophilic inflammation. Xanthine oxidase is involved in purine catabolism and hyperuricemia, not the downstream inflammatory cascade.

qs.q: Which complement component is primarily responsible for marking fungal cells for phagocytosis?
qs.e: C3b acts as an opsonin, tagging fungal cells for phagocytosis, while C5a is a chemotactic factor.
qs.s: Mycoses: Fungal Pathogenesis, Virulence & Host Immune Defense: MCQs

qs.q: Which morphological form of dimorphic systemic fungi is specifically responsible for resisting phagocytosis at body temperature in infected tissues?
qs.e: The yeast form is the parasitic tissue form found at body temperature (37°C) and resists phagocytosis. The mold or filamentous form typically exists at cooler environmental temperatures.
qs.s: Medical Virology: Adenoviruses, Hemorrhagic Fever & Viral Receptors: MCQs

qs.q: Which chemical factor found in lung secretions acts as an opsonin to promote the phagocytosis of pathogens?
qs.e: Surfactants in the lungs act as opsonins to promote the phagocytosis and enhanced clearance of pathogens by immune cells. Defensins are antimicrobial proteins that disrupt microbial membranes rather than acting as opsonins.

qs.q: Opsonization enhances the phagocytosis of bacteria by immune cells. How does this process occur with antibody-coated bacteria?
o: Antibodies activate the bacterial cell wall synthesis.
Antibodies trigger the release of bacterial toxins.
Antibodies block the bacterial surface receptors, preventing immune cell attachment.
Antibodies bind to Fc receptors on phagocytes, facilitating engulfment.
qs.e: Opsonization involves antibodies attaching to bacteria, which then allows these antibody-coated bacteria to bind to Fc receptors on phagocytes like macrophages. This interaction significantly enhances the efficiency of phagocytosis and bacterial destruction.

qs.q: Which structural component of Streptococcus pneumoniae is primarily responsible for preventing phagocytosis and serves as the main target for vaccines?
qs.e: The polysaccharide capsule is the most critical virulence factor, preventing phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils, and forms the basis of current vaccines. Peptidoglycan provides structural integrity rather than primary anti-phagocytic protection.
qs.s: Streptococcus pneumoniae: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features and: MCQs

qs.q: Protein A is a surface protein found in the cell wall of Staphylococcus aureus. It has a high affinity for the Fc region of IgG antibodies, leading to the opsonization of bacteria in a way that prevents effective phagocytosis.
o: The Fc region of IgG antibodies
The Fab region of IgG antibodies
qs.e: Protein A, a virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus, binds to the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies. This binding interferes with opsonization and phagocytosis by preventing the antibody's Fc region from interacting with phagocytic cells.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Microbiology Exam - June 12, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which of the following types of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) is particularly specialized for the phagocytosis, degradation, and presentation of particulate antigens (e.g., bacteria, cellular debris) to T cells, especially in later stages of immune responses?
qs.e: Macrophages are highly phagocytic cells that are crucial for clearing pathogens and cellular debris. They can also process and present antigens, particularly particulate antigens, to activated T cells.

ai.title: Phagocytosis in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Phagocytosis is the cellular process by which immune cells engulf and destroy pathogens. Clinicians must recognise when defects or evasion strategies lead to infection, and choose appropriate antibiotics and supportive care.

sections.p: Phagocytosis is performed mainly by neutrophils, macrophages and dendritic cells. It involves chemotaxis, adhesion, engulfment, and intracellular killing. The process is essential for clearing bacteria, fungi, parasites and cellular debris.
b: Dendritic cells: bridge to adaptive immunity

sections.p: Many bacteria have evolved mechanisms to resist phagocytosis: capsules, endotoxins, and surface proteins that inhibit opsonisation. Virulent strains of *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Staphylococcus aureus* are classic examples.
b: Protein A binds Fc region of IgG

sections.p: Pathogens reach phagocytes via bloodstream, mucosal surfaces or direct inoculation. In low‑resource settings, malaria parasites, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and HIV compromise phagocyte function.
b: Malaria: parasites survive in hepatocytes and erythrocytes, evading splenic clearance
TB: macrophage infection leads to granuloma formation
HIV: CD4+ T‑cell loss impairs macrophage activation

sections.p: Defective phagocytosis predisposes to severe bacterial infections, sepsis, and opportunistic infections. Common presentations include pneumonia, septicemia, and chronic granulomatous disease.
b: Pneumonia in diabetics: impaired neutrophil chemotaxis
Granulomatous disease: caseating granulomas in TB

sections.p: Clinical suspicion is guided by history of immunosuppression, recurrent infections, or atypical presentations. Laboratory tests confirm phagocyte function and identify causative organisms.
b: If cultures unavailable, use empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics guided by local resistance patterns.

t.b: Assesses ability to generate reactive oxygen species; a negative result suggests chronic granulomatous disease.
Identifies bloodstream pathogens; a positive result in a neutropenic patient indicates impaired clearance.
Low levels may indicate consumption by ongoing infection or congenital deficiency.
Detects parasites that evade splenic phagocytosis; a positive smear in a febrile patient warrants antimalarial therapy.

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection and support phagocyte function. Antibiotics target the organism; adjunctive therapy may include colony‑stimulating factors or immunoglobulin.
b: Avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics in renal impairment; monitor renal function closely.

t.b: Provides passive antibodies to opsonise pathogens when endogenous production is inadequate.
Stimulates bone marrow to produce neutrophils, improving chemotaxis and phagocytosis.

sections.p: Remember that phagocytosis is the first line of defence; defects manifest as recurrent, severe infections. In low‑resource settings, empirical therapy must balance efficacy and toxicity.
b: In malaria, splenic sequestration leads to hypersplenism; treat with antimalarials and consider splenectomy if refractory.

t.b: First‑line artemisinin‑based combination; monitor for haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

faq.q: What is the role of the respiratory burst in neutrophils?
faq.a: It generates reactive oxygen species that kill engulfed bacteria inside the phagosome.

faq.q: How does a capsule protect bacteria from phagocytosis?
faq.a: It prevents complement deposition and antibody binding, blocking opsonisation.

faq.q: Why are diabetics more prone to infections?
faq.a: Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis and microbial killing.
